Cross-validation is a more sophisticated version of training and testing a model. For cross-sectional data, one approach to cross-validation is to select a single observation for the test set and use the remaining observations for the training set. Compute the error on the test observation and repeat this step for all observations. Compute the forecast accuracy measures based on the errors obtained. This makes efficient use of the available data, as only one observation is omitted at each step. For time series data, the training set can only include observations prior to the test set. Suppose k observations are needed to produce a reliable forecast; then the process works as follows: Starting with i=1, select the observation k + i for the test set, and use the observations at times 1, 2, ..., k+i–1 to estimate the forecasting model. Compute the error on the forecast for k+i. Repeat the above step for i = 1,2,..., N where N is the total number of observations.

The Cook Political Report's Partisan Voting Index (PVI) is a measure of how strongly a U.S. congressional district leans toward the Democratic or Republican Party. It is based on the methodology introduced by Rob Richie of the Center for Voting and Democracy in the Center's July 1997 Monopoly Politics report. The index looks at how every congressional district voted in the past two presidential elections combined and compares it to the national average. The Cook PVI is displayed as a letter, a plus sign, and a number, with the letter (either a D for Democratic or an R for Republican) indicating the party that won the district and the number showing how many percentage points above the national average it received.

In 2022, the Cook Political Report updated its formula for calculating PVI values to weigh the most recent presidential election more heavily.

Transgender people have the right to medical privacy. According to the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA), medical providers and insurance companies are prohibited from disclosing any personal medical information including a person's transgender status. HIPAA also allows transgender people to access and receive a copy of their medical records from health care facilities.

However, transgender people may face discrimination in healthcare settings, known as "trans broken arm syndrome". This occurs when a doctor mistakenly assumes that a trans person's medical ailments stem from their trans status or gender-affirming care and consequently treats their problem incorrectly or denies them care entirely. A 2022 survey from the Center for American Progress revealed that 19 percent of trans individuals had experienced this form of discrimination in the past year.

It can also be difficult for transgender people to find insurance coverage for their medical needs. Even though there is medical consensus that hormone therapy and sex reassignment surgery (SRS) are medically necessary for many transgender people, the kinds of health care associated with gender transition are sometimes misunderstood as cosmetic, experimental or simply unnecessary. This has led to public and private insurance companies denying coverage for such treatment.

Cross-validation is a more sophisticated version of training and testing a model. For cross-sectional data, one approach to cross-validation is to select observation i for the test set, and use the remaining observations in the training set. Compute the error on the test observation and repeat the above step for i = 1,2,..., N where N is the total number of observations. Compute the forecast accuracy measures based on the errors obtained. This makes efficient use of the available data, as only one observation is omitted at each step. For time series data, the training set can only include observations prior to the test set. Suppose k observations are needed to produce a reliable forecast; then the process works as follows: Starting with i=1, select the observation k + i for the test set, and use the observations at times 1, 2, ..., k+i–1 to estimate the forecasting model. Compute the error on the forecast for k+i. Repeat the above step for i = 1, 2, ..., N-k.

Cross-validation is a more sophisticated version of training and testing a model. For cross-sectional data, one approach to cross-validation is to select an observation for the test set and use the remaining observations for the training set. Compute the error on the test observation and repeat this step for all observations. Compute the forecast accuracy measures based on the errors obtained. This makes efficient use of the available data, as only one observation is omitted at each step. For time series data, the training set can only include observations prior to the test set. Suppose k observations are needed to produce a reliable forecast; then the process works as follows: Starting with i=1, select the observation k + i for the test set, and use the observations at times 1, 2, ..., k+i–1 to estimate the forecasting model. Compute the error on the forecast for k+i. Repeat the above step for i = 1,2,..., N where N is the total number of observations.

The Cook Political Report's Partisan Voting Index (PVI) is a measure of how strongly a U.S. congressional district leans toward the Democratic or Republican Party. It is based on the methodology introduced by Rob Richie of the Center for Voting and Democracy in the Center's July 1997 Monopoly Politics report. The index looks at how every congressional district voted in the past two presidential elections combined and compares it to the national average. The Cook PVI is displayed as a letter, a plus sign, and a number, with the letter (either a D for Democratic or an R for Republican) indicating the party that won the district and the number showing how many percentage points above the national average it received.

In 2022, the Cook Political Report updated its formula for calculating PVI values to weigh the most recent presidential election more heavily.

Medical providers and insurance companies are prohibited from disclosing any personal medical information, including a person's transgender status. However, transgender people may face discrimination in healthcare settings, known as "trans broken arm syndrome." This occurs when a doctor mistakenly assumes that a trans person's medical ailments stem from their trans status or gender-affirming care and consequently treats their problem incorrectly or denies them care entirely. Shelta is a cant language, a type of secret language used by traveling people and traditionally by Irish Travellers. It is also known as the Cant or the Gammon. The language is characterized by its heavy use of Irish loanwords and its unique phonetic system. For example, the Shelta word for 'man' is luchrán, which is derived from the Irish word luchorpán, meaning 'leprechaun.' Many words are complex by incorporating numerous consonants within, as in the word skraꭕo for 'tree, bush' with the consonant /ꭕ/ being a hissing sound that is held in the back of the throat, and is held longer than other consonants. Loanwords Some Shelta words have been borrowed by mainstream English speakers, such as the word "bloke" meaning 'a man' in the mid-19th century. Orthography There is no standard orthography. Broadly speaking, Shelta can either be written following an Irish-type orthography or an English-type orthography. For example, the word for 'married' can either be spelled lósped or lohsped; the word for 'woman' can either be spelled beoir or byohr. Cross-validation is a more sophisticated version of training and testing a model. For cross-sectional data, one approach to cross-validation is to select an observation for the test set and use the remaining observations for the training set. Compute the error on the test observation and repeat this step for all observations. Compute the forecast accuracy measures based on the errors obtained. This makes efficient use of the available data, as only one observation is omitted at each step. For time series data, the training set can only include observations prior to the test set. Suppose k observations are needed to produce a reliable forecast; then the process works as follows: Starting with i=1, select the observation k + i for the test set, and use the observations at times 1, 2, ..., k+i–1 to estimate the forecasting model. Compute the error on the forecast for k+i. Repeat the above step for i = 1,2,..., N-k where N is the total number of observations.

The Cook Political Report's Partisan Voting Index (PVI) is a measurement of how strongly a U.S. congressional district leans toward either the Democratic or Republican party. It is based on the methodology introduced by Rob Richie of the Center for Voting and Democracy in 1997 and is updated every two years. The PVI is calculated by looking at how every district voted in the past two presidential elections and comparing it to the national average. It is displayed as a letter, a plus sign, and a number, with the letter indicating the party that won the district and the number showing how many percentage points above the national average it received.

In 2022, the Cook Political Report updated its formula for calculating PVI values to weigh the most recent presidential election more heavily.

In healthcare settings, transgender individuals may experience discrimination known as "trans broken arm syndrome," in which medical providers mistakenly assume that a trans person's medical ailments stem from their trans status or gender-affirming care. This can lead to incorrect treatment or denial of care. According to a 2022 survey from the Center for American Progress, 19 percent of trans individuals had experienced this form of discrimination in the past year.

Transgender people have the right to medical privacy, and medical providers and insurance companies are prohibited from disclosing personal medical information, including a person's transgender status, under the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA). HIPAA also allows transgender people to access and receive a copy of their medical records from healthcare facilities.

Finding insurance coverage for medical needs can be difficult for transgender people. Even though hormone therapy and sex reassignment surgery (SRS) are medically necessary for many transgender people, insurance companies may deny coverage for such treatment, often misunderstanding them as cosmetic, experimental, or unnecessary. However, courts have recognized gender dysphoria as a legitimate medical condition constituting a "serious medical need."
